abstract: The interplay between natural selection, gene flow, and geography is a key driver of population differentiation. This study investigates their influence on the recent adaptive radiation of Heliconius cydno, a mimetic and aposematic butterfly with striking variation in wing color pattern across its distribution in Central and northern South America. The genetic basis of this phenotypic diversity has a modular architecture, whereby a few key genes and cis-regulatory elements control differences among morphotypes. Using whole-genome sequences from 133 individuals representing all subspecies of H. cydno, we investigated (1) the role of Andean orogeny in its diversification and (2) the genetic basis of the variation in the hindwing white submarginal band, which to date, had remained unknown. First, we found that five of the fourteen described subspecies correspond to distinct monophyletic lineages and well-defined genetic clusters that originated in northwestern South America and later expanded into Central America and the Colombian inter-Andean valleys. Second, we observed signatures of genetic structure that were consistent with geographic patterns, particularly those associated with the inter-Andean region and Gorgona Island. Third, we identified ivory:mir-193 as the locus underlying variation in the white submarginal band on the hindwing. We also detected evidence of introgression suggesting that this trait was likely transferred from H. cydno to H. melpomene, contributing to the establishment of a novel mimicry ring with H. erato. Altogether, these findings highlight the roles of geography, genomic architecture, and introgression in the diversification of H. cydno.
